---
title: "The Geometry of Motion — Volume II: Control Is Motion"
description: "Develops geometric mechanics and nonlinear control for feasible motion, disturbance response, and impact outcomes."
---

**Volume II: Control Is Motion** connects the geometric tools of Volume I to the design and analysis of movement. For a golf swing, the question is how the body and club can produce a desired impact outcome through a feasible motion, and how sensitive that outcome is to variation.

Configuration, timing and control must be considered together. Traversing the same configuration path at a different speed changes velocity, inertial loads and required effort. Ground and grip constraints restrict compatible motion; available inputs limit which accelerations can be produced. Impact evaluates the resulting motion at an event whose time may itself change under a perturbation.

## The 'Control Is Motion' Paradigm

For a declared smooth control-affine mode, a nominal trajectory needs a compatible admissible input:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot{x}_d(t)&=f(x_d(t),t)+G(x_d(t),t)u_d(t),\\
u_d(t)&\in\mathcal{U}(x_d(t),t).
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $x_d$ is the nominal state, $u_d$ the input, $f$ the drift field and $G$ the input matrix field. State and contact constraints must also hold. This is a model for one smooth mode; actuator states and contact transitions require their own equations when included.

Regulation, tracking, path following, event objectives and orbital stabilization are complementary task specifications. A finite golf swing need not be a periodic orbit, and an along-path perturbation can still alter impact speed or contact time. Transverse analysis requires valid phase coordinates and the terms introduced by a moving basis. A local linear calculation can guide feedback design; a nonlinear funnel additionally requires verification over its stated region, input limits, disturbances and relevant transitions.

The chapters develop these connections through derivations and worked model examples. The closing golf case study sets out a proposed investigation. Numerical consistency, a verified statement about a declared model, and experimental validation of human movement are distinct forms of evidence.
